The Friday We Promised · Everything Is On Track, Book 1

Chapter 1

About 15 minutes of reading.

The banner had come loose over the coffee machine. Only the left end was still attached, so that WELCOME TO FRIDAY hung at a slope, the last two letters folded into the drip tray.

It was Monday.

Lena put her bag down and reached above the machine. The tape held. Someone had used the good tape, the kind you couldn’t get off painted walls without taking a little of the room with it.

“Leave it,” Marcus said. “It knows something.”

He was carrying two mugs and a paper plate with half a cinnamon roll on it. The frosting had picked up a brown crescent from the coffee in his right hand.

“You’ve had four days to take this down.”

“Not my workstream.”

She gave him a look.

“I was saving that one for you.” He offered her the unoccupied corner of the plate. “Go on. It’s the middle.”

“I don’t want your breakfast.”

“That’s what makes it generous.”

She tore off a small piece. The bread was cold. There was something cheering about eating from a paper plate someone else was still holding, and she let herself enjoy it before looking through the kitchen glass at the meeting room.

Three people were already there. One stood to move a chair out of her usual place.

“Are we doing this?” Marcus asked.

He didn’t mean the meeting.

“We’re doing the review.”

“Right.” He shifted the mugs so she could take one. “It’s a lovely review. Everybody’s talking about it.”

The coffee he had brought her had milk in it. He remembered. She had stopped buying milk for the apartment because it went sour before she could finish it, and some mornings this small accommodation could make her want to tell him more than he had asked.

“How’s your crew?”

“Dani wants an answer before she changes the weekend schedule again.”

“I’ll speak to her.”

“She doesn’t need a visit. She needs an answer.”

“I know.”

He was still watching her. She looked past him into the meeting room and took her bag off the counter.

The room had spent two weeks preparing to hear no. She could tell from the neatness of the table. The old printouts were gone. Somebody had wiped away the half moon left by a water glass. They had made it easy for her to postpone them in a clean room.

Marcus followed her gaze. “Calvin says I’m not allowed to help him move this weekend unless I can swear I won’t keep checking my phone.”

“Can you?”

“Obviously. I can swear to anything.”

That got half a laugh out of her. “Tell Dani I’ll have the date after this meeting.”

“The real date?”

“Marcus.”

“That’s a no, then.”

She took the paper plate from him, folded the uncovered cinnamon roll inside it, and set it on top of the refrigerator where he would forget it. He had not asked whether the hold-control work was done. He knew it wasn’t. What he wanted was the same thing everyone wanted: a fact sturdy enough to build a weekend around.

“I need you to give me a clean view of the manual work,” she said. “Not the answer you think the room can live with.”

“I gave you the clean view Friday.”

“You gave me a range.”

“Because work comes in a range. It’s one of its most annoying qualities.”

“Give me what changed.”

He rubbed his thumb over the seam of his cup. “Two people I thought I had, I don’t have. One can do Saturday afternoon if we pay her. One has a kid thing he didn’t tell me about because apparently I’m the kind of manager people protect from children.”

“We can pay Saturday.”

“You can ask Adrian to pay Saturday.”

“I can get it.”

“I know you can.” He said it with enough affection that she almost missed the fatigue. “That’s not the same as the work being small.”

The meeting room door opened. Adrian looked out, saw them, and tapped two fingers against his watch.

Lena picked up both coffees. Marcus retrieved the cinnamon roll from the refrigerator without looking at her.

“After the meeting,” she said.

“I love the future. Everybody has coverage in the future.”

In the meeting room, Adrian was leaning against the windowsill with his jacket over a chair. He was listening to somebody on his phone. When he saw Lena he held up a finger, then covered the mouthpiece.

“Tell me we’re not doing another date meeting.”

He said it lightly. Around the table, two people laughed quietly, the way people do when they are finally allowed to admit something.

“We’ve got the reconciliation results,” Lena said.

“Good.” He went back to the call, nodded once, and ended it. “Good. Sit down.”

The screen at the end of the room still showed the invitation from the previous meeting. The projected date was last Friday. Lena put her laptop on the table and closed that window before anybody could comment on it.

Priya came in carrying no laptop, just a notebook and her phone. She took the chair nearest the screen rather than the one beside Lena. That was probably about the cable. Lena noticed it anyway.

“Morning,” she said.

“Morning. I sent the separate holds list at eight.”

“I saw.”

“All of it?”

Lena looked up. Priya’s expression hadn’t changed. She could have meant the attachment, which had been divided into two files. Lena decided that was what she meant.

“Yes. Both files.”

Adrian pulled his chair in. “Before we get into detail, I need to tell the service partner whether we’re buying the extension.”

“I know.”

“I’m not saying we shouldn’t. I need an answer.”

Marcus sat with his coffee between his palms. The cinnamon roll was gone. Everybody had brought something into this room that depended on what she said: a schedule, a bill, a reason to keep promising their own people that this was nearly over. Through the kitchen glass she could see the banner’s loose end trembling under the air vent.

“Friday,” she said.

Adrian let his shoulders drop. It was such a small movement that she might have imagined it if she hadn’t seen the same relief travel around the table.

She hadn’t meant to give them the word by itself. There were two sentences she had intended to put before it.

“Subject to the controls we’re reviewing,” she added.

“Of course.” Adrian opened the notebook in front of him. “That’s what we’re here for.”

Priya set her phone face down.

Someone at the far end of the table made a quiet joke about finally canceling the cancellation meeting. The laugh that followed was brief and grateful. Lena opened the deck while it moved through the room. For one bright second, they had all looked relieved to see her.

For a moment Lena was irritated with Priya. She knew how unfair that was. Priya had done the work; her attachment had arrived early; she was entitled to prefer the conditions to the date. But she could have let them have the relief for thirty seconds.

“The balances reconcile,” Lena said, bringing up the first slide. “Every account in the agreed population. That’s real progress, and I don’t want us to lose it in the things we still need to fix.”

Marcus lifted his mug an inch. Adrian said, “Absolutely.”

Priya waited until Lena looked at her.

“The balances,” she said. “What about the instructions that decide when we take the payments?”

“I was coming to that.”

Lena advanced the slide. There were two hundred and fourteen accounts in the next table. She had read both attachments. She knew what was in them.

At the top of the table, the heading from the previous draft still said TEMPORARY CONTROL. She had asked for that heading herself because EXCEPTION had made the room feel as though the thing had already happened.

“We have a discrete population,” she said. “We know who they are. The financial positions came across correctly. The collection holds need separate confirmation.”

Collection holds. Lena had stopped hearing the phrase months ago. Each row in that table was a person who had called servicing after losing hours or a job or a partner’s income, and had been told, by someone with a calm voice, that nothing would come out of their account until their review. Some of those people had planned rent around the sentence.

“In the live process,” Priya said.

“Yes.”

“Not confirmation that the list exists.”

Lena kept her hand on the wireless presenter. “Yes, Priya.”

“I’m not correcting you. I’m making sure the action is clear.”

“Then let me finish making it clear.”

Nobody moved. The irritation rose hot along Lena’s neck, out of proportion to the interruption. She could hear herself sounding like someone who had been contradicted when, technically, Priya had only specified the noun.

She put the presenter down.

“The account balances and schedules reconcile,” she said. “That proves we moved the loans correctly. It doesn’t prove the new system knows which two hundred and fourteen customers we promised not to charge. We confirm that separately, before the first payment file goes out on Monday.”

Priya made one mark in her notebook.

“Is that accurate?” Lena asked.

“Yes.”

The answer gave her none of the pleasure she had expected from forcing it into the room.

Adrian turned to Priya. “What would make it inaccurate?”

He asked questions this way when he wanted to know which problem he was buying. It was one of the things Lena had learned from him: let the person with the concern draw the fence, then decide what you could afford inside it.

Priya uncapped her pen. “If the readiness statement says the control is complete because the balances match. Or if we treat the hold list as proof that the new process will respect it. Do we agree those are different facts?”

“And what do you need by Friday?”

“Evidence that each active hold is on the live payment instruction. The one that actually takes the money.” She looked at Lena, not Adrian. “And checked by someone other than the person who entered it. Is that unreasonable?”

Marcus lowered his mug. “That is not one job.”

“I didn’t say it was.”

“It sounds like one job when you say it before nine in the morning.”

Priya looked at him. “It is two before breakfast.”

“After breakfast, usually.”

Adrian did not smile, but Lena saw him decide not to stop them. Marcus’s jokes were tolerated most when the room needed him to volunteer something unpleasant.

“Marcus gave me a range Friday,” Lena said. “He’s updating it today. The plan includes entry and independent checking.”

“The range assumed the straightforward cases,” Marcus said.

She turned to him. “It included an allowance.”

“An allowance is what you give a child. I gave you an average with ugly ends.”

“Fine. Update the ends.”

“That’s what I just agreed to do.”

His tone stayed mild. The small victory of getting him to name the work had somehow become his victory.

Adrian slid his notebook closer. “How many people?”

“That depends which part you’re asking about,” Marcus said.

“The part that gets us to Friday without inventing a second Thursday.”

Marcus looked at Lena. She knew he wanted her to repeat what he had said in the kitchen: two people lost, paid Saturday coverage, skill that could not be manufactured by assigning a name. If she repeated all of it now, Friday would become a discussion again. If she left it for his updated estimate, she was respecting the request for actual numbers rather than narrating his problem for him.

She chose the version that let the room keep moving.

“I need paid coverage for the people Marcus identifies,” she said. “And I need the borrowed staff held through the weekend if their own directors agree.”

“Names and hours by noon,” Adrian said. “I’ll protect it in principle now. I’m not signing an empty timesheet.”

“I wouldn’t ask you to.”

“You have, but you called it contingency.”

The room laughed, including Lena. Adrian had let her ask for money without making the request look desperate.

Marcus did not laugh. He turned his coffee cup so the paper seam faced away from his thumb.

“I’ll give you the names,” he said. “Dani gives me the skill split. I’m not guessing who can check a hardship arrangement because they attended a migration briefing.”

“Good,” Adrian said. “Then don’t.”

Marcus’s mouth changed slightly, distrust interrupted by relief.

Lena moved to the next slide. It showed two columns: reconciled items in green and remaining work in amber. The colors had seemed honest at eleven the previous night. In daylight, the green occupied enough of the screen to make the amber look decorative.

Priya leaned forward. “Can those be separate results?”

“They are separate columns.”

“They are under one heading.”

The heading was MIGRATION READINESS. Lena had written it herself.

“They need to come together somewhere,” she said. “Adrian can’t make two release decisions about one migration.”

“He may have to make two decisions at different times. Move the platform Friday. Submit the first collection file Monday.”

Adrian glanced from the slide to Priya. “Is that what you’re recommending?”

“I’m saying the evidence supports different statements. The platform can reconcile while the collection control remains open.”

“Which means?”

“Don’t let the first statement certify the second.”

Lena could feel the meeting trying to split into the kind of argument that ended with everyone agreeing to revise a document and no one agreeing what would happen. She stood and went to the whiteboard.

“All right.” She drew a horizontal line. Above it she wrote RELEASE. Below it, FIRST FILE. “We track both. We do not use the reconciliation result as hold confirmation. I will join them in the readiness account and keep the conditions explicit.”

Priya watched her write. “Join them how?”

“With separate evidence and one recommendation.”

“Whose?”

“Mine,” Lena said.

“That’s right,” Adrian said.

There it was: the shape of the opportunity he had been giving her all year. Not the title, though there was one now, head of delivery, on the agenda of a promotion committee that met next week. Not the money, which had appeared as a range in an email she had pretended to read only once. This was the real advancement. A problem arrived in pieces, and Lena was the person trusted to return with one usable account of it.

Adrian closed his notebook. “Friday remains the working date. Marcus, names and actual coverage. Priya, give Lena the exact evidence you need. Lena, bring me the joined view tomorrow. If the facts don’t support Friday, I need to know before we spend another day acting as if they do.”

“You will.”

She said it before Marcus could look at her.

People began collecting phones and cups. The meeting had ended early, a rare proof that something had been decided. Adrian stopped beside Lena at the board.

“Good call,” he said quietly. “A date makes the remaining work possible.”

“The remaining work makes the date possible.”

“Also true.” He handed her the cap she had left on the tray. “That’s why you get the glamorous job of making both sentences fit.”

When he left, Lena erased a small black mark beneath FIRST FILE. She had drawn the line too hard and the ink had bled into an old scratch. Priya was still at the table, closing her notebook.

“Send me your wording before you circulate it,” Priya said.

“I always do.”

“Last time you sent it at eleven forty.”

“It was still before circulation.”

Priya put the notebook in her bag. “That’s technically true.”

She left before Lena could decide whether the remark was funny.

On the slide, Lena changed the heading to TWO CONDITIONS / ONE READINESS ACCOUNT. Then she opened the action list and typed her own name beside the only line that did not yet have an end time.

By six, the warmth had gone out of the windows. Sun still lit the upper floors across the street, but at ground level the wind pushed wrappers along the curb and found the space between Lena’s coat and her neck.

She was halfway to the parking ramp when Tessa called.

“You’re walking,” Tessa said.

“Hello to you, too.”

“You breathe differently when you’re walking.”

Lena stopped breathing for half a second, which made Tessa laugh.

“I’m going to my car.”

“At six?”

“Some of us leave work.”

“Then you can hear me.”

Lena shifted her laptop bag higher on her shoulder. A bus went past, stirring grit from the gutter. “What’s wrong?”

“Nothing is wrong. I’m calling before something is wrong, which I thought was the kind of behavior your people encouraged.”

“My people.”

“The ones who put words like proactive on glass walls.”

“We don’t have glass walls.”

“Never mind.”

Lena stepped into the ramp. Fluorescent light flattened the concrete and made every car look abandoned. She heard a metal tray strike something on Tessa’s end, followed by her sister saying, away from the phone, “No, the other rack. The one that doesn’t try to kill you.”

“Are you working?” Lena asked.

“I run a bakery. I don’t wait beside a telephone for my older sister to have emotional availability.”

“You called me.”

“And look how well it’s going.”

There were voices behind Tessa, the hiss of the espresso machine, a burst of laughter that ended when someone remembered a customer could hear. Lena pictured the narrow back counter dusted with flour no one had time to wipe properly until closing. Tessa never sounded most tired when she was tired. She became efficient and cheerful, as if daring the day to charge her for either quality.

“The landlord finally booked the pipe work,” Tessa said. “Monday morning. He needs the rear dry-storage wall clear before the contractor comes.”

“The wall with the leak?”

“The wall that he has recently agreed may, in rare weather conditions, become damp.”

“Tess.”

“Yes, the wall with the leak. I have to get the bottom shelves out and move the labeled bins into the loading area. Saturday, eight to ten. I need you for two hours.”

Lena reached her car and did not unlock it yet. “This Saturday?”

“There is only one before Monday.”

“We’re migrating Friday.”

“I know. I’ve met Friday. Friday has been coming for six weeks.”

“It was postponed twice.”

“I remember. You canceled dinner for both of them.”

Lena could have said the first cancellation came at lunch. She did not.

The old argument waited between them, fully furnished. Lena could have walked into it without turning on a light. She pressed the unlock button. Her car answered with two hard flashes.

“The move finishes Friday night,” she said. “Saturday is stabilization. I won’t need to be there in the morning.”

She had no basis for the last sentence. There was a difference, though, between having no basis and being wrong. The coverage she had asked Adrian to protect existed precisely so the whole project did not continue to depend on her body occupying a room.

“I didn’t ask whether they need you,” Tessa said. “I’m asking whether I have you.”

“Yes.”

“Eight.”

“I’ll be there at eight.”

“Until ten.”

“Do you think I’m going to disappear at nine forty-five?”

Tessa said nothing.

“That was a joke,” Lena said.

“It wasn’t a new one.”

Lena put her bag in the passenger seat. “Eight to ten. What do you need me to bring?”

“Old clothes.”

“Do you have enough containers?”

“Yes.”

“I can pick up the clear stackable ones from that place by you.”

“No containers.”

“If you’re moving dry goods—”

“I have containers, Lena. I need one person with arms.”

“I have arms.”

“I’ve seen them. They’re very managerial.”

Lena laughed, and Tessa did too, though hers ended first.

“I need to know because if you can’t, I can put Maya on the counter and pay Chris to come in,” Tessa said. “Chris wants the hours. I don’t have another two hours in payroll this week, but I can find it if I know now.”

“You don’t need to call Chris.”

“Okay.”

Tessa was granting the promise rather than resting on it.

Lena got into the car. The closed door muted the ramp to a low mechanical hum.

“How bad is the wall?” she asked.

“It ruined two cartons of pastry boxes. Not the food. The boxes that cost more than food because they have a little window in them.”

“Can you charge them to the landlord?”

“I can send him a picture. He can send me a sentence containing the word unfortunately.”

“Send me the lease.”

“No.”

“I can look at the maintenance language.”

“You can come Saturday and lift the shelves.”

“I can do both.”

“I need you to do the one thing I asked.”

Lena started the engine. “How are you getting home?”

“Maya’s closing. I’m doing the supplier order, then Theo’s picking me up.”

Theo was a new name or an old name newly promoted. Lena searched the last two conversations and found nothing she could ask without revealing she had forgotten something.

“Good,” she said.

Tessa waited just long enough for the word to become strange. “Yes. It is.”

“I’ll see you Saturday.”

“Eight o’clock. In clothes you can ruin. Don’t bring a project plan.”

“What if I wear one?”

“Then I charge you for coffee.”

After they hung up, Lena opened her calendar. Saturday contained a pale block from seven until noon: MIGRATION STABILIZATION: HOLD. She changed its end time to seven forty-five and moved it to the narrow space before Tessa’s request. The calendar warned her that the two events were in different locations. She turned off travel time, saved TESSA: STORAGE, 8:00–10:00, and sent the invitation.

Then she added a ten-fifteen check-in for the migration team.

Lena has promised Friday. Now the week begins.
